questions.stem: About 2% of extracted invoice records (roughly 500 a week) are rejected by the ERP importer with JSON parse errors. The cause is usually a trailing comma, or an unescaped quote in a supplier name such as `Smith "Bros" Ltd`. The prompt says "Return JSON matching this structure", followed by one example record. Finance wants rejections at zero, not just lower. What is the most reliable fix?

options.text: Extend the example with tricky cases, such as quotes and commas in names, and add explicit escaping instructions.
options.why: This targets the observed failures but only lowers the rate, and Finance wants zero.

options.text: Use an extraction tool whose `input_schema` is the invoice schema, and require that tool via `tool_choice`.
options.why: Tool use with a JSON schema eliminates syntax errors.

options.text: Run every output through a JSON-repair library before the ERP, and log any record it can't repair.
options.why: Repair can silently alter values, and some records will still fail.

options.text: Set temperature to 0, so the model consistently produces the well-formed structure it gets right 98% of the time.
options.why: Lower temperature doesn't guarantee well-formed output.

questions.explanation: `tool_use` with an input schema is the most reliable way to get syntactically valid structured output.

questions.stem: Schema-enforced tool use has removed every JSON syntax error. A month later, Finance reports a different problem: about 1.5% of records put the invoice date in `due_date`, or record a tax amount as a line total. The product manager asks, "I thought the schema guaranteed correct data, so why didn't it catch this?" What is the accurate answer, and the right next step?

options.text: The schema isn't in strict mode. Strict mode makes the model validate field meanings as well as types.
options.why: Strict mode enforces structure. It doesn't validate meaning.

options.text: The model sometimes ignores the schema under load, so structure should be re-validated on receipt.
options.why: Structure is being followed correctly. The values are wrong.

options.text: Schemas guarantee structure and types, not meaning. Add semantic checks (due ≥ issue date, totals reconcile) and clearer guidance.
options.why: Schemas remove syntax errors, and semantic errors need validation and better prompting.

options.text: The two date fields look alike to the model. Renaming them `date_a` and `date_b` would remove the confusion.
options.why: Less descriptive names make the confusion worse.

questions.explanation: Schemas give syntax and shape. Semantic errors need validation, retry and better instructions.

questions.stem: About a third of bills of lading are for loose cargo and have no container number. The schema marks `container_number` as a required string. An audit found plausible-looking but invented container numbers in 6% of loose-cargo records, and some passed the ISO 6346 check digit by chance. Customs penalties for false container data are severe. What is the best schema change?

options.text: Keep the field required, and add a regex for the ISO 6346 format to reject invented values.
options.why: The question notes that some invented numbers already pass format checks.

options.text: Make `container_number` nullable or optional, and instruct the model to return `null` when it is absent.
options.why: A required field with no source data pressures the model to fabricate one.

options.text: Keep it required with a default of `"UNKNOWN"` that the model uses for loose cargo.
options.why: A magic string pollutes downstream data, and `null` is the honest representation.

options.text: Drop the field from the main schema, and run a separate optional extraction pass for containerised shipments.
options.why: This adds a pass and complexity when a nullable field solves the problem directly.

questions.explanation: Make fields nullable or optional when the source may lack them, so the model isn't pushed to fabricate.

questions.stem: `document_type` is an enum: `invoice`, `bill_of_lading`, `customs_form`. Over the last month, suppliers started sending packing lists and credit notes, and those are being forced into the existing categories. Credit notes classified as `invoice` were posted as charges, and finance had to reverse 37 of them. More new document types are expected. What is the best fix?

options.text: Replace the enum with a free-text field, so the model can describe new document types accurately as they appear.
options.why: This loses the consistency that downstream routing depends on.

options.text: Add `packing_list` and `credit_note` now, and add new values as they show up in production.
options.why: This helps today, but each future type will be misrouted until someone notices.

options.text: Add `other` (with a `document_type_detail` string) and `unclear`, and route those values to review.
options.why: Escape-hatch values prevent forced misclassification of types nobody anticipated.

options.text: Instruct the model to choose the closest matching type when a document doesn't fit any category exactly.
options.why: That forced choice is how credit notes were posted as charges.

questions.explanation: Include `other` plus a detail field, and `unclear`, in enums for cases outside the known categories. Add known new types as well.

questions.stem: A validator finds that line items don't sum to the subtotal on 4% of invoices. A manual review of 100 of these found 83 extraction mistakes (a missed row, or a misread 7 vs 1) and 17 genuine supplier errors. Today every mismatch goes to human review, and the queue is three days behind. What is the most effective automated recovery?

options.text: Retry with the document plus the specific error, such as "items sum to 1,240.00 but subtotal read as 1,420.00".
options.why: Feeding back the specific error fixes most extraction mistakes, and genuine supplier errors still fail and go to review.

options.text: Re-run extraction with the same prompt up to three times, and accept the first result that passes validation.
options.why: Retrying without feedback often repeats the same misreading.

options.text: Overwrite the subtotal with the computed line-item sum, since 83% of mismatches are extraction errors.
options.why: This would hide the 17% that are real supplier errors.

options.text: Keep routing every mismatch to humans, and add reviewers until the backlog clears.
options.why: This ignores an automated fix that would resolve most of the backlog.

questions.explanation: Validation-retry loops should feed back the specific error, and unresolved cases should still escalate.

questions.stem: Some scanned customs forms fail validation because the HS tariff code is missing. After three retries, each with the exact validation error fed back, 92% of these still fail. Reviewers confirm that on those scans the HS code box is blank or cut off by the scanner. The pipeline's retry limit is configurable. What should happen next for such records?

options.text: Raise the retry limit to ten with stronger wording, in case the model can find the code elsewhere on the form.
options.why: This wastes cost and raises the risk that the model eventually invents a code.

options.text: Fill in the supplier's most frequently used HS code from past records, and flag the record as low confidence.
options.why: This fabricates regulated data, even with a flag.

options.text: Stop retrying, since the data isn't in the source. Route these records to human review with the reason.
options.why: Retries can't recover information that isn't in the document.

options.text: Re-run with a larger model and higher-resolution images, so it can read fine print the current setup misses.
options.why: Reviewers confirmed the box is blank or cut off, so there is nothing to read.

questions.explanation: Retry loops have limits. When the source lacks the data, escalate rather than retry.

questions.stem: Finance wants to catch invoices where the printed total doesn't match the line items, whatever the cause (an extraction mistake or a supplier error). For disputes, it must also keep exactly what the supplier printed. The current schema has one `total` field. What schema design best supports this?

options.text: Extract `stated_total` and `calculated_total` plus a `conflict_detected` flag, and have code check and route conflicts.
options.why: Both values are kept and the discrepancy is explicit, so code can verify it.

options.text: Extract `total` as printed, and have a downstream ERP job recompute the line sum and compare.
options.why: This works partly, but the comparison happens late and without extraction context.

options.text: Extract `total`, and instruct the model to correct it when the line items don't add up, noting the correction.
options.why: This alters the record, and loses the printed value needed for disputes.

options.text: Extract only line items and let the ERP compute totals, so model arithmetic is never trusted.
options.why: This loses the printed total needed for disputes.

questions.explanation: Design schemas with self-check fields (stated versus calculated, conflict flags) that code can verify.

questions.stem: Field accuracy is 98% on the five most common invoice layouts, but under 70% on rare ones, such as multi-page tables, totals printed at the top, and two-column Japanese invoices. Together, rare layouts are about 12% of volume. The prompt has three few-shot examples, all common layouts, and is near the team's token budget. Errors on rare layouts are mostly fields left `null` or values taken from the wrong table column. Which improvement helps most?

options.text: Add 20 more examples of common layouts, to reinforce the extraction pattern the model handles well.
options.why: This reinforces what already works and blows the token budget.

options.text: Add a paragraph explaining that layouts vary and that totals and tables may appear in unexpected places.
options.why: This describes the problem without showing how to handle it.

options.text: Route rare layouts automatically to human review, since they are only about 12% of volume.
options.why: That's about 3,000 documents a week sent to people for a segment that can be improved.

options.text: Swap some common-layout examples for rare ones (multi-page, totals-first, two-column), within the same budget.
options.why: Examples covering structural variety improve generalisation within the budget.

questions.explanation: Few-shot examples should span the variety of document structures the system encounters.

questions.stem: The weekly backlog of 25,000 documents must be extracted before finance close at 09:00 Monday. The team chose overnight batch processing for the 50% saving. Recent batches finished in 40–70 minutes, and the validation-retry step adds about 2 hours. A developer suggests submitting at 05:00 Monday "to keep data fresh". What is the sound operating approach?

options.text: Submit at 05:00 Monday as suggested, since recent batches finished in about an hour and there is margin.
options.why: Typical completion isn't guaranteed. There is no latency SLA, and the window can be up to 24 hours.

options.text: Submit so a full 24-hour window plus retries still meets 09:00 Monday, use `custom_id`, and resubmit failures only.
options.why: Plan to the worst case rather than the typical case, and retry selectively.

options.text: Run validation-retry loops inside each batch request with multi-turn tool calls, so results return final.
options.why: Batch requests don't support multi-turn tool loops.

options.text: Split by document type into three batches without IDs, and match results back by their order.
options.why: Result order isn't a reliable key, so use `custom_id`.

questions.explanation: Batch SLA arithmetic: allow up to 24 hours, correlate by `custom_id`, and resubmit failures only.

questions.stem: A revised extraction prompt adds handling for credit notes and changes three field instructions. It looked good on 15 hand-picked documents. The team wants to use it for this week's full 25,000-document batch, which costs about $1,900 even at batch pricing. What should they do first?

options.text: Run the full batch now, since batch pricing makes it affordable, then compare against last week's run.
options.why: A flawed prompt wastes the full spend, and the fix needs a second full run.

options.text: Skip further testing, since schema enforcement guarantees the new output will be valid for the ERP.
options.why: Schemas don't guarantee that the extracted values are correct.

options.text: Run a representative sample, measure accuracy by document type, fix problems, then run the full batch.
options.why: 15 hand-picked documents aren't representative. Refine on a sample before scaling.

options.text: Run the full batch synchronously instead, so problems surface early and the run can be stopped.
options.why: This doubles the cost, and it is still the wrong order of work.

questions.explanation: Iterate on a representative sample, then scale. This is a stated batch best practice.

questions.stem: A validation run on 2,000 labelled documents shows 97% field-level accuracy overall. Leadership wants to auto-post every record from next month. The data science lead notes that scanned customs forms are only 8% of volume, and that the run included few non-English documents. What is the main risk in leadership's conclusion?

options.text: 97% is below the 99.5% benchmark for financial data, so no part of the pipeline is ready for automation yet.
options.why: Some segments may already be safe, so the analysis needs to break results down by segment.

options.text: The aggregate can hide weak segments such as scanned forms or non-English documents. Validate by type, language and field first.
options.why: Aggregate accuracy masks weak segments, which the lead's observations point to.

options.text: Field-level accuracy overstates quality, so only document-level accuracy should be used for the decision.
options.why: Document-level accuracy helps, but it still doesn't reveal which segments are weak.

options.text: There's no material risk, since 97% beats the accuracy of the manual entry clerks the pipeline replaces.
options.why: This ignores segment variance and the cost of errors in specific fields.

questions.explanation: Break accuracy down by document type, language and field before deciding what to automate.

questions.stem: Automation is live for invoices and bills of lading, about 20,000 auto-posted records a week. About 40 new suppliers onboard each month, often with unfamiliar layouts. Leadership asks how quality will be monitored over time when reviewers can audit only about 300 records a week. What should the team do?

options.text: Audit only records the model marked low confidence, since that's where errors are most likely.
options.why: Records the model was confidently wrong about would never be audited.

options.text: Audit the first 300 records processed each Monday, a consistent weekly sample at fixed cost.
options.why: Not random, and biased toward particular suppliers and batches.

options.text: Audit a stratified random sample of 300 across document types, suppliers (including new ones) and languages.
options.why: Stratification keeps every segment visible, including new suppliers.

options.text: Stop auditing after three consecutive months above target, and re-audit only after an incident.
options.why: New suppliers and layouts bring drift that would go unnoticed.

questions.explanation: Stratified random sampling keeps quality visible across all segments.

questions.stem: Today every customs form, about 4,000 a week, goes to human review. The team wants to use per-field confidence to send only the risky ones. A pilot using the model's raw confidence routed 600 forms, but a later audit found real errors in 9% of the forms it auto-posted. Which TWO steps are required for this routing to work? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Calibrate the scores on a labelled validation set, so each threshold maps to a known error rate.
options.why: Raw confidence demonstrably failed in the pilot, and calibration fixes that.

options.text: Route low-confidence fields, and records whose validations contradict each other, to human review.
options.why: This is the routing policy that calibration makes trustworthy.

options.text: Keep the model's raw confidence but lower the threshold until more forms are routed.
options.why: Uncalibrated thresholds just trade one unknown error rate for another.

options.text: Use one global threshold for every field and document type, so the routing rule is easy to audit.
options.why: Calibration differs by field and segment, so one untested threshold misroutes.

options.text: Send only high-confidence forms for spot-checks, since low-confidence ones will be retried anyway.
options.why: That is backwards.

questions.explanation: Field-level confidence calibrated on labelled data, plus routing of low-confidence or contradictory items, makes review efficient.

questions.stem: Customs packets are 80–120 pages and are processed in one request. Fields on the first 5 and last 5 pages are extracted with about 97% accuracy. Fields in the middle pages, such as consignee details on page 47, come out at about 71%. The packets have consistent section boundaries: cover, commercial invoice, packing list, certificates. Which mitigation is most appropriate?

options.text: Repeat the full field list at the end of the prompt, so the model is reminded after reading the packet.
options.why: This may help slightly, but it doesn't fix weak attention over the middle pages.

options.text: Raise `max_tokens`, so the model has room to output every field found in the packet.
options.why: This controls output length, not attention over the input.

options.text: Split by section, extract from each separately, then merge (or lead with a summary of key sections and their headers).
options.why: This counters lost-in-the-middle and uses the consistent section boundaries.

options.text: Instruct the model to read every page carefully and not skip any section of the packet.
options.why: This is vague guidance that doesn't change how attention is distributed.

questions.explanation: Mitigate lost-in-the-middle by chunking, putting key information first, and using section headers.

questions.stem: A bill of lading lists a gross weight of 12,400 kg on page 1 (the header) and 14,200 kg on page 3 (the cargo manifest). The customs declaration depends on this figure, and misdeclaration fines start at €5,000. Most suppliers are consistent, and conflicts like this appear in about 0.3% of documents. In past conflicts, the header was right about 60% of the time and the manifest about 40%. The extraction currently has one `gross_weight_kg` field and keeps whichever value it reads first. What should the extraction record?

options.text: The page-1 header value, since headers on bills of lading are authoritative, with a note that page 3 differs.
options.why: This applies an arbitrary rule and still treats the record as final.

options.text: Both values with their page numbers and a conflict flag, with the record sent to review rather than picking one.
options.why: Provenance is kept, the conflict is surfaced, and a person decides.

options.text: The higher value, since over-declaring weight is the safer error and avoids under-declaration penalties.
options.why: This is arbitrary, and over-declaring is also a misdeclaration.

options.text: The mean (13,300 kg) with a lowered confidence score, so the record can still be auto-posted.
options.why: This invents a value that neither page states.

questions.explanation: When sources conflict, keep both values with provenance and flag the conflict for review.

questions.stem: The pipeline enriches records by calling the MCP tool `lookup_supplier(tax_id)`. It fails in three ways: the extracted tax ID is malformed (about 1%), the supplier registry is briefly down (several times a week), or the pipeline lacks permission for restricted suppliers. All three currently return `null`, and the pipeline treats `null` as "new supplier", creating duplicate supplier records. How should the tool respond?

options.text: Return `null` in all three cases, but have the pipeline check the tax-ID format first, which catches the malformed case.
options.why: This fixes one of the three causes. Outages and permission failures still look like new suppliers.

options.text: Retry inside the tool with exponential backoff until it succeeds, so callers always receive a supplier record.
options.why: Malformed and permission failures never succeed on retry.

options.text: Return a placeholder supplier marked "pending enrichment", so records post and get corrected later.
options.why: This creates exactly the kind of bad supplier records already causing trouble.

options.text: Return `isError: true` with a category per case (validation, transient and retryable, permission) and a clear message.
options.why: With distinct categories, the pipeline can fix the input, retry, or escalate as appropriate.

questions.explanation: Structured MCP error categories drive the right recovery, and stop failures being mistaken for valid empty results.
